title: Docker Volumes, Networks & Registries
description: Persist data with volumes, configure container networking, and use Docker registries.

terms.definition: A Docker-managed directory stored outside the container filesystem. Volumes persist data even when the container is removed.
A host directory mounted into a container. Useful for development when you want live code reloading.
The networking or storage backend Docker uses. Examples include bridge, host, overlay, and local.
A service that stores and distributes Docker images. Docker Hub is the default public registry.

data.text: Containers are ephemeral. When a container is removed, anything written to its writable layer is gone. **Volumes** are the recommended way to persist data generated by containers — they live outside the container lifecycle and survive removal.

cards.title: Named Volumes
cards.description: Managed by Docker in a host directory. Best for databases and persistent data.
pros: Easy to back up or migrate
cons: Slightly higher overhead than bind mounts

cards.title: Bind Mounts
cards.description: Mounts a specific host directory into the container. Good for code syncing in development.
cons: Host-specific paths break on other machines

cards.title: tmpfs Mounts
cards.description: Stores data in memory only, never written to disk. Ideal for secrets.

data.title: Creating and using a volume
data.content: Create a named volume manually, then mount it into a container.
data.code:
docker volume create my-app-data
docker run -d \
  --name myapp \
  -v my-app-data:/app/data \
  my-image:latest

data.title: Volume inspection and cleanup
data.content: List, inspect, and remove volumes to keep your system tidy.
data.code:
docker volume ls
docker volume inspect my-app-data
docker volume rm my-app-data
docker system prune -a --volumes

data.text: Docker provides several **network drivers** for different use cases. By default, containers on the same host can communicate, and Docker's built-in DNS resolves container names to their IPs.

rows: Default; containers on the same host connect here
Skip container networking; use the host directly
Assign a MAC address from the host to the container

data.title: Custom bridge network
data.content: Create a dedicated network so containers can communicate securely by name.
data.code:
docker network create my-net
docker run -d --name app --network my-net my-app
ocker run -d --name redis --network my-net redis:7-alpine

data.text: A **Docker registry** stores and serves Docker images. Docker Hub is the default public registry, but you can also use private registries like AWS ECR, Google GAR, GitHub Container Registry, or self-hosted registries.

items: **Search** — Find official images on Docker Hub: `docker search nginx`
**Tag** — Give a local image a registry-specific name: `docker tag myapp myuser/myapp:1.0`
**Push** — Upload to a registry: `docker push myuser/myapp:1.0`
**Pull** — Download from a registry: `docker pull myuser/myapp:1.0`

data.title: Tagging and pushing to Docker Hub
data.content: Authenticate, tag, and push your image so others can pull it.
data.code:
docker login

docker tag my-app john/example-app:1.0
docker push john/example-app:1.0

data.title: Use digests for immutable deployments
data.text: When you push an image, Docker generates a content-addressable digest (e.g., `sha256:abc123...`). Referencing images by digest guarantees that every environment runs the exact same image.

Private registries are essential for production workloads. They let you control who can read or write images, store proprietary code, and integrate with your CI/CD pipeline. Most cloud providers offer managed registry services with authentication tied to your cloud account.

data.title: Set up volumes and networks
data.description: Practice creating a custom network and attaching a named volume to a container.
steps: Create a named volume: `docker volume create app-data`
Create a custom bridge network: `docker network create app-net`
Run a Redis container on that network with the volume mounted: `docker run -d --name redis --network app-net -v app-data:/data redis:7-alpine`
Run a second container on the same network and verify it can reach Redis by name.
Remove both containers and confirm the volume still exists: `docker volume ls`
data.expectedOutcome: You should understand how volumes persist data and how custom networks enable DNS-based service discovery.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Named volumes persist data beyond the container lifecycle; bind mounts are best for development code sync.
Docker's bridge network driver isolates containers; custom networks provide DNS-based service discovery.
Registries store and serve images — tag and push images so they can be pulled in any environment.
Reference images by digest for reproducible, immutable deployments.
data.takeaway: Volumes, networks, and registries are the glue that connects containers across environments.
